title: Berkshire 2008 letter: buying in fear, float, derivatives, and admitting mistakes
summary: Buffett's 2008 letter covers Berkshire's four goals, insurance float that cost less than zero, and buying when pessimism reigns. He owns up to his own errors (ConocoPhillips, Irish banks), warns against derivatives, history-based models and Black-Scholes at long durations, and says he won't trade sleep for extra profit.

principles.text: When investing, pessimism is your friend and euphoria the enemy; buy quality when it is marked down.
principles.quote: When investing, pessimism is your friend, euphoria the enemy.

principles.text: Insurance float is valuable when underwriting is profitable, because the money is held and invested at negative cost.
principles.quote: This means that our $58.5 billion of insurance “float” – money that doesn’t belong to us but that we hold and invest for our own benefit – cost us less than zero.

principles.text: Keep ample liquidity; never risk sleep or survival for extra profit or rely on others' kindness.
principles.quote: We never want to count on the kindness of strangers in order to meet tomorrow’s obligations. When forced to choose, I will not trade even a night’s sleep for the chance of extra profits.

principles.text: Be the buyer of choice by deserving it: keep promises, avoid leverage, give managers autonomy, hold through thick and thin.
principles.quote: That means we must keep our promises; avoid leveraging up acquired businesses; grant unusual autonomy to our managers; and hold the purchased companies through thick and thin (though we prefer thick and thicker).

principles.text: Be skeptical of history-based models; their assumptions can fail when current conditions differ from the past.
principles.quote: Investors should be skeptical of history-based models.

principles.text: Approval is not the goal of investing; applause can sedate the brain and block re-examining conclusions.
principles.quote: Approval, though, is not the goal of investing. In fact, approval is often counter-productive because it sedates the brain and makes it less receptive to new facts or a re-examination of conclusions formed earlier.
